title: Benchmarking Evidence Retrieval and Reasoning for Financial AI Systems
abstract: We introduce FinRCA-Bench, a benchmark that separates retrieval failure from reasoning failure in financial question answering. The benchmark pairs filings, earnings transcripts and analyst notes with questions whose evidence is known, so a wrong answer can be attributed to the retriever or to the reasoner. Across eleven large language models we find that most reported gains come from retrieval rather than reasoning, and that reasoning accuracy saturates well below human analysts.

title: Do Banks Really Know What They Get From AI?
abstract: Using supervisory data on technology spending at 340 bank holding companies, we ask whether banks can measure the return on their artificial intelligence investments. Disclosed benefits are concentrated in cost centres that were already being automated, and we find no relationship between reported AI spending and subsequent efficiency ratios.

title: Correlated AI Forecasts and Systemic Risk
abstract: When many institutions run the same forecasting model, their portfolio adjustments become correlated. We build a general equilibrium model in which a common predictor raises the probability of a fire sale, and calibrate it to mutual fund holdings. Concentration of model providers, not model accuracy, is what drives the systemic externality.

title: Language Models for Earnings Call Sentiment
abstract: We compare fine-tuned language models against dictionary methods on a corpus of earnings call transcripts, and evaluate whether the resulting sentiment scores predict post-announcement drift. The models beat dictionaries in classification accuracy but their advantage in return prediction disappears after transaction costs.
